lead_characters.name: Bobby
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s to 30s, working-class, New York-based, white or ethnicity unspecified in the excerpt.

lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Ray Liotta in Goodfellas — a fast-talking, volatile guy whose charm and panic are always in the same frame, giving an actor room for swagger, humiliation, and sudden menace.

lead_characters.name: Lara
lead_characters.hook: Lara is the clean break Bobby can't bully, flatter, or joke his way out of. She speaks plainly, sees the mess in the house and in the relationship, and leaves with enough composure to make Bobby's denial look pathetic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-stealing exit role that gave Michelle Williams in Blue Valentine its sting — a grounded, emotionally legible woman who gets the moral high ground without becoming a speechifying device.

lead_characters.name: Carmy
lead_characters.demographics: Male, age unclear, likely Bobby's criminal associate or boss.
lead_characters.hook: Carmy is the voice on the other end of the line who cuts through Bobby's excuses and brings the pressure back down to one thing: get the money. He reads as an off-screen force with authority, impatience, and a relationship to Bobby that is already loaded.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of terse, authority-heavy supporting role that lets an actor do a lot with very little, similar to the pressure-cooker energy of Michael Stuhlbarg in A Serious Man — a voice that can dominate a scene without needing pages.
